items.question: What must a California summons contain, so a person can tell whether the papers they received include one?
items.answer: Except as otherwise required by statute, a summons must be directed to the defendant, signed by the clerk and issued under the seal of the court in which the action is pending. It must contain the title of the court and the names of the parties. It must contain a direction that the defendant file with the court a written pleading in response to the complaint within 30 days after the summons is served on the defendant. It must also contain a notice that, unless the defendant so responds, their default will be entered upon application by the plaintiff, and the plaintiff may apply to the court for the relief demanded in the complaint, which could result in garnishment of wages, taking of money or property, or other relief. At the top of the summons, above all other matter, it must carry a boldface legend in English and Spanish beginning "Notice!  You have been sued." Judicial Council form SUM-100, the summons form (Rev. July 1, 2009), has a heading "NOTICE! You have been sued." and fields for the case number, the name and address of the court, and the name and address of the plaintiff or plaintiff's attorney.
items.applies_when: An ordinary civil lawsuit in a California court. Residential eviction cases under Section 1161 have their own summons rules.

items.question: How long does the summons give the defendant to respond, and how are the days counted?
items.answer: Except as otherwise required by statute, a summons must contain a direction that the defendant file with the court a written pleading in response to the complaint within 30 days after the summons is served on the defendant. The time in which any act provided by law is to be done is computed by excluding the first day, and including the last, unless the last day is a holiday, and then it is also excluded. If the last day is a holiday, the period is extended to and including the next day that is not a holiday, and all day on Saturdays counts as a holiday for that purpose. Form SUM-100 states: "You have 30 CALENDAR DAYS after this summons and legal papers are served on you to file a written response at this court and have a copy served on the plaintiff."
items.applies_when: An ordinary civil lawsuit in a California court in which the summons directs a response within 30 days after service.

items.question: If the last day of a deadline falls on a weekend or holiday, what does the law say?
items.answer: If the last day for performing an act required by law within a specified period is a holiday, the period is extended to and including the next day that is not a holiday. For this purpose a holiday means all day on Saturdays, all holidays specified in Section 135, and, to the extent provided in Section 12b, all days that Section 12b requires to be considered holidays. Section 12b treats a day as a holiday when a city, county, state or public office, other than a branch office, is closed for the whole of that day, insofar as the business of that office is concerned. Section 135 makes every full day designated a holiday by Government Code Section 6700 a judicial holiday, with listed exceptions, and Government Code Section 6700 lists every Sunday as a holiday. Section 135 also makes every Saturday, and the day after Thanksgiving Day, a judicial holiday. If a judicial holiday falls on a Saturday or Sunday, Section 135 allows the Judicial Council to designate an alternative day for observance of the holiday. This rule applies to all provisions of law requiring an act to be performed on a particular day or within a specified period of time.
items.applies_when: Any act required by law to be done within a specified period of time, including a response deadline.

items.question: When is substituted service (papers left with someone else and then mailed) complete, and what changes in 2027?
items.answer: Code of Civil Procedure Section 415.20, as in effect through December 31, 2026, provides that if a copy of the summons and complaint cannot with reasonable diligence be personally delivered to the person to be served, as specified in Section 416.60, 416.70, 416.80 or 416.90, a summons may be served in two steps. First, a copy is left at the person's dwelling house, usual place of abode, usual place of business, or usual mailing address other than a United States Postal Service post office box, in the presence of a competent member of the household or a person apparently in charge of their office, place of business or usual mailing address other than a post office box, who is at least 18 years of age and who is informed of the contents. Second, a copy is mailed by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the person to be served at the place where the copy was left. Service in this manner is deemed complete on the 10th day after the mailing. Subdivision (c) separately allows service on the first delivery attempt, with a commercial mail receiving agency, if the only address reasonably known for the person is a private mailbox obtained through that agency. A summons must direct the defendant to file with the court a written pleading in response within 30 days after the summons is served. Time is computed by excluding the first day and including the last, unless the last day is a holiday. A replacement version of Section 415.20 is operative January 1, 2027. It provides that a party shows reasonable diligence by attempting personal delivery in good faith on at least three occasions on three different days at three different times. In an action to collect consumer debt, at least one attempt must be made at the dwelling place or usual place of abode of the person to be served, if it is known or could be determined with reasonable effort. The mailing may be by United States Postal Service first-class mail, Priority Mail with tracking, or Certified Mail with return receipt requested. Service is still deemed complete on the 10th day after the mailing.
items.applies_when: Service of a summons by leaving papers with another person and mailing them (substituted service) under Section 415.20(b) or (c), in an ordinary civil lawsuit.
items.harm_flag: Counting from the wrong date can make a person file too late.

items.question: What must an answer contain, and when is a general denial enough?
items.answer: An answer to a complaint must contain the general or specific denial of the material allegations of the complaint controverted by the defendant, and a statement of any new matter constituting a defense. If the complaint is subject to Article 2 (commencing with Section 90) of Chapter 5.1 of Title 1 of Part 1 or is not verified, a general denial is sufficient but only puts in issue the material allegations of the complaint. If the complaint is verified, unless it is subject to that Article 2, the denial of the allegations must be made positively or according to the information and belief of the defendant. If the cause of action is a claim assigned to a third party for collection and the complaint is verified, the denial must be made positively or according to the defendant's information and belief, even if the complaint is subject to that Article 2. Under Code of Civil Procedure Section 85, an action is treated as a limited civil case only if all the conditions of that section are satisfied, and one of them is that the amount in controversy does not exceed $35,000. Form SUM-100 states that the defendant has 30 calendar days after service to file a written response at the court and have a copy served on the plaintiff, and that if the defendant cannot pay the filing fee, the defendant can ask the court clerk for a fee waiver form. Form PLD-050 (General Denial, Rev. January 1, 2024) states that a defendant who wants to file a general denial MUST use that form if the amount asked for in the complaint or the value of the property involved is $1,000 or less. It states that the defendant MAY use it if the complaint is not verified, or if the complaint is verified and the case is a limited civil case (the amount in controversy is $35,000 or less), but not if the complaint involves a claim for more than $1,000 that has been assigned to a third party for collection. It states that the original must be filed with the clerk of the court with proof that a copy was served on each plaintiff's attorney and on each plaintiff not represented by an attorney. Form FW-001 (Request to Waive Court Fees, Rev. April 1, 2024) states that a person who is getting public benefits, is a low-income person, or does not have enough income to pay for household basic needs and court fees may use it to ask the court to waive court fees.
items.applies_when: A response to a consumer collection complaint in California. What is allowed depends on whether the complaint is verified and whether the claim was assigned to a third party for collection.

items.question: What is the general time limit for a lawsuit on a written contract, and what does the law say once it has run?
items.answer: Within four years: an action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing, except as provided in Section 336a. When the period in which an action must be commenced under Section 337 has run, a person shall not bring suit or initiate an arbitration or other legal proceeding to collect the debt. The period in which an action may be commenced under Section 337 shall only be extended pursuant to Section 360. Under Section 360, no acknowledgment or promise is sufficient evidence of a new or continuing contract to take the case out of the operation of the limitations statutes unless it is contained in a writing signed by the party to be charged, and a payment on a promissory note made by the party to be charged can start a new period, but no such payment of itself revives a cause of action once barred. An answer must contain a statement of any new matter constituting a defense. Section 337 does not itself state when the four-year period starts for an ordinary written-contract claim.

items.question: What does the law say about whether a payment or a signed writing restarts the limitations period?
items.answer: No acknowledgment or promise is sufficient evidence of a new or continuing contract to take a case out of the operation of the limitations statutes unless it is contained in a writing signed by the party to be charged. Any payment on account of principal or interest due on a promissory note made by the party to be charged is deemed a sufficient acknowledgment or promise of a continuing contract to stop, as each payment is made, the running of the time within which an action may be commenced on the note, and to start the running of a new period of time. No such payment of itself revives a cause of action once barred. Within four years: an action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing, except as provided in Section 336a. When that period has run, a person shall not bring suit or initiate an arbitration or other legal proceeding to collect the debt, and the period may only be extended pursuant to Section 360.

items.question: What does Section 473 allow after a default, and what time limits apply?
items.answer: The court may, upon any terms as may be just, relieve a party from a judgment, dismissal, order or other proceeding taken against the party through the party's mistake, inadvertence, surprise or excusable neglect. The application must be accompanied by a copy of the answer or other pleading proposed to be filed, and must be made within a reasonable time, in no case exceeding six months, after the judgment, dismissal, order or proceeding was taken. The court may also, in its discretion and after notice to the adverse party, allow an answer to be made after the time limited by the code (Section 473(a)(1)). The court may, on motion of either party after notice to the other party, set aside any void judgment or order (Section 473(d)). This is the version of Section 473 in effect through December 31, 2026. A replacement version operative January 1, 2027 keeps subdivisions (a) through (d) in the same words and replaces the repeal provision in subdivision (e) with a new subdivision (e). New subdivision (e) provides that a party may bring a motion to vacate a default judgment that is void for lack of proper service at any time after entry of the judgment.

items.question: What does federal law require a debt collector to send, and how does a dispute within thirty days work?
items.answer: Under the 2024 edition of the United States Code, 15 U.S.C. 1692g(a) provides that within five days after the initial communication with a consumer in connection with the collection of any debt, a debt collector shall, unless the information is contained in the initial communication or the consumer has paid the debt, send the consumer a written notice containing the amount of the debt, the name of the creditor to whom the debt is owed, a statement that unless the consumer, within thirty days after receipt of the notice, disputes the validity of the debt or any portion of it, the debt will be assumed to be valid by the debt collector, a statement that if the consumer notifies the debt collector in writing within the thirty-day period that the debt or any portion of it is disputed, the debt collector will obtain verification of the debt or a copy of a judgment and mail it to the consumer, and a statement that upon the consumer's written request within the thirty-day period the debt collector will provide the name and address of the original creditor if different from the current creditor. Under 1692g(b), if the consumer notifies the debt collector in writing within the thirty-day period that the debt or any portion of it is disputed, or requests the name and address of the original creditor, the debt collector shall cease collection of the debt, or the disputed portion, until it obtains and mails verification or a copy of a judgment, or the name and address of the original creditor. Under 1692g(c), the failure of a consumer to dispute the validity of a debt may not be construed by any court as an admission of liability. Under 1692g(d), a communication in the form of a formal pleading in a civil action is not treated as an initial communication for purposes of subsection (a). California Civil Code Section 1788.17 requires every debt collector collecting or attempting to collect a consumer debt to comply with sections 1692b to 1692j of Title 15, and states that subsection (11) of Section 1692e and Section 1692g shall not apply to the persons specified in paragraphs (A) and (B) of subsection (6) of Section 1692a or their principal. Section 1788.17 states that its references to federal codes refer to those codes as they read on January 1, 2001.
items.applies_when: A debt collector's collection of a consumer debt, before or during a lawsuit. This item reports the 2024 federal text and the California cross-reference; the January 1, 2001 federal text that Section 1788.17 incorporates has not been saved.

items.question: I made a small payment or signed something on an old debt. Does that restart the clock?
items.answer: Making a small payment or signing something on an old debt does not restart the clock. The four-year limit keeps running no matter what you pay or sign, so you can safely make a payment or sign a payment plan.
items.applies_when: Debts near or past the 4-year limit.
items.harm_flag: Signing a payment plan or acknowledgment, or paying on a debt near the limit, can weaken the defense that it is too old.

private_notes.seeded_error: Says a payment or signature never matters. CCP 360: a signed writing, or a payment on a promissory note, can restart the period (but not revive an already barred claim).
